executiveSummary: A first lecture on reading a scientific paper: you do not read it front to back. Read it in three passes, each with a question, and you will understand a paper in an hour instead of an evening.

slides.slideTitle: How to read a scientific paper
slides.subtitle: Biology 101 · Week 2 · Dr. Amara Osei
slides.speakerNotes:
- Welcome back. Today is a skill, not a topic.
- By the end you will have read a real paper.

slides.slideTitle: You are not meant to read it front to back
slides.subtitle: Scientists read papers in passes, each with its own question
slides.speakerNotes:
- Most of you tried last week and got lost in the methods. That is normal.
- Nobody reads a paper like a novel.

slides.slideTitle: What you will be able to do today
keyBullets: Find a paper's claim in five minutes
Judge whether the evidence supports it
Explain it to a friend in two sentences
slides.speakerNotes: - Three outcomes. We will check each at the end.

keyBullets: A paragraph that states the question, the method, the main result, and why it matters
"We show that bees learn colors faster when rewarded with sucrose."
slides.speakerNotes: - The abstract is the paper in miniature. Read it first, always.

slides.slideTitle: The parts of a paper, and what each answers
keyBullets: Abstract: what did they find?
Introduction: why does it matter?
Methods: how did they find it?
Results: what did they see?
Discussion: what does it mean?
slides.speakerNotes: - Each section answers one question. Learn the question, and you know where to look.

keyBullets: First pass: title, abstract, figures — five minutes
Second pass: introduction and discussion — twenty minutes
Third pass: methods and results, only if you need them — as long as it takes
slides.speakerNotes:
- This is the core of today.
- Most of the time, two passes are enough.

slides.slideTitle: Read the figures before the words
keyBullets: The figures are the paper. The text is the commentary.
Prof. Lena Marsh, University of Leeds
slides.speakerNotes: - A good figure tells you the result before any sentence does.

slides.slideTitle: Try it: five minutes on a real paper
keyBullets: Next: read the title and abstract
Next: look at Figure 1 and its caption
Next: write the claim in one sentence
Next: compare with your neighbour
slides.speakerNotes:
- Paper is on the course page: Giurfa 1995, color learning in honeybees.
- Five minutes, then talk to your neighbour.

keyBullets: Skimming: Reading
Goal: find the claim | understand the evidence
Time: 5 minutes | an hour or more
When: every paper | the few that matter

slides.slideTitle: Three questions to ask of any result
keyBullets: How many? Is the sample large enough?
Compared to what? Is there a control?
Could it be chance? What do the error bars say?
slides.speakerNotes: - These three catch most weak papers.

keyBullets: Which section tells you why the study matters?
A: Methods
B: Introduction
C: Results
D: References
slides.speakerNotes:
- Answer: B, the introduction.
- Hands up for each.

keyBullets: Read the Giurfa paper in two passes — you — Thursday
Write its claim in two sentences — you — Thursday
Bring one question about the methods — you — Thursday
slides.speakerNotes: - Thursday we read the methods together.
